en: Oṃ.
(Offstage: Ho there, you celestial beings! Let auspicious rites be performed!
Victorious is the venerable Sage Kauśika, the disciple of Kṛśāśva; now, in this world, the warrior lineage of the thousand-rayed Sun triumphs.
Victorious is the moon of the solar dynasty, the protector of the worlds, who bears the vow of bestowing fearlessness upon the universe and who subdues the enemies of the Kṣatriyas. //1//

(Then enter Śūrpaṇakhā and Mālyavān, agitated, in a celestial chariot. Mālyavān: Child, have you seen the unification of the gods, in that Indra and the others have come of their own accord to offer salutation?
Śūrpaṇakhā: What you have discerned does not contradict [the truth]. Now I am trembling; so what is to be done here?

Mālyavān: That Queen Kaikeyī, the mother of Bharata, who was previously granted two boons by King Daśaratha—her maidservant named Mantharā, who is a messenger from Ayodhyā to Daśaratha, has been dispatched to Mithilā and is currently staying in the vicinity of Mithilā; this was just now reported to me by my spies. You must enter her body and act in such and such a manner.
(Thus he whispers in her ear.
Śūrpaṇakhā: What do you think he will actually do? What indeed is his intention?
Mālyavān: Our virtuous conduct within the Ikṣvāku lineage would not be compromised, especially in the case of such a seeker of victory.
Śūrpaṇakhā: And then what?

Mālyavān: Therefore, by this method of the practitioners of yoga (*yogācāra*), having drawn him very far away and brought him into the lap of the Rākṣasas, it would be easy to launch attacks upon him as he wanders through the Vindhya forests, being ignorant of the terrain. For Virādha, Danu, Kabandha, and others will roam as fierce predators within the sacrificial grounds of the Daṇḍaka forest. Indeed, the power of resolve (*utsāha-śakti*) can be undermined through deception once the power of sovereignty (*prabhu-śakti*) has been lost. Moreover, Rāvaṇa’s determination to take Sītā for himself is irreversible;
and thus, this plan is both easily executed and purposeful.
Śūrpaṇakhā: But even with Lakṣmaṇa as my companion, what is the purpose?
Mālyavān:
That hero, a master of weapons, is to be regarded as equal to Rāma;
for the employment of a deceptive punishment is the same toward one as it is toward both. (2)

Śūrpaṇakhā: This is indeed distressing to me; it is not right that he should disregard it. For it is improper to bring about the presence of the descendant of Daśaratha while he is far away, and it is impossible to settle a woman’s enmity with one who has no prior cause for hostility.

Mālyavān: He is indeed very close by virtue of his proximity to the earth. How could the slayer of Tāṭakā—who, along with his followers, caused the destruction of Sunda and Upasunda—be without enmity? Furthermore, the hostility between Rāma and Rāvaṇa is unavoidable even otherwise. Behold: he has the world to protect, while we are the eternal, forceful commanders of the world. Under such circumstances, what kind of conciliation can there be with one who is constantly hostile and does what is disagreeable? What ends does the joy of the Raghus pursue, since he was chosen as their lord by the gods themselves? Therefore, there is no peace here, nor any lack of division; his arrows are his only means. (3)
Even against a superior enemy, neither punishment nor open warfare should be displayed;
rather, silent punishment must be employed, and this is its preliminary approach.

That being the case, what else could he do after the abduction of Sītā? Furthermore: "If his wife has been seized by enemies, even if he is ashamed and seeks refuge in death—or even otherwise—he is as good as dead when crushed, devoid of majesty; yet, though tormented, he might still enter into an alliance. (5)
If he should rise up to slay us with a fury matured by humiliation, the ocean will not be able to restrain its flow, for it possesses the power of the sun;
however, that enemy shall be struck down by the terrible monkey, the son of the Wielder of the Thunderbolt, who is possessed of fearsome energy and has previously assumed the friendship of Rāvaṇa.
And by means of this incidental discussion, much more remains to be investigated.
Śūrpaṇakhā: What is it like?

Mālyavān: My child, you are dear to Rāvaṇa and you understand what must be done; therefore, my heart's distress is told to you without hesitation. Because he dwells upon the earth, Rāma is an enemy by his very nature as a Kṣatriya, constantly intent on doing us harm in two ways [as both a neighbor and an oppressor].
Furthermore, my third grandson is the natural-born enemy of the Lord of the Night-rangers (Rāvaṇa); like a serpent due to its proximity, he generates fear in us. (7)

Kumbhakarṇa, though alive, was as good as dead due to his addiction to feigned sleep and his lack of discipline; Vibhīṣaṇa, however, was endowed with the personal qualities that attract subjects, and thus the people were devoted to him.

Kharadūṣaṇa and Triśiras, whose conduct is consistent with their lineage, attend upon the king; for they milk the king of his wealth as one milks a cow with a calf. Once incited, the subjects will turn against him. Thus, this royal family, already shattered by internal dissension, will be broken as soon as it is attacked by Rāma. As it has been said: "Even a minor point of vulnerability, when exploited, becomes difficult to overcome for one under attack. And in that matter, there is a remedy through the restraint of Vibhīṣaṇa.

But neither open punishment (*prakāśadaṇḍa*), nor silent punishment (*tūṣṇīndaṇḍa*), nor confinement (*saṃrodhana*), nor banishment (*apasāraṇa*) would be appropriate. In that regard, how could the Rākṣasas—who share an inseparable bond with him—endure open punishment? Even silent punishment, when inferred by the wise, would provoke the subjects and lead to a disastrous end if Rāma were the one to attack. If, however, confinement were carried out as a form of humiliation, then Khara and the others, out of their singular friendship for him, would revolt. They would even surround him as he was being exiled; therefore, Khara and the others must be considered first. (8)
In that regard, Rāma is of use.

Śūrpaṇakhā: Oh, how great is the weight of servitude! For although the family connection is equal for Rāvaṇa and those headed by Khara, my maternal grandfather thinks in such a way [favoring the former].
Mālyavān: Such is the conduct of a son of noble family.
Śūrpaṇakhā: What will Vibhīṣaṇa’s response be toward Khara and the others?
Mālyavān: This wise one, having himself perceived the impending calamity, will surely withdraw on his own. However, we must not disregard him by thinking that this danger is merely internal. For:
"Having cultivated friendship from childhood, he will certainly seek refuge with Sugrīva on Mount Ṛṣyamūka, which was granted as a land-portion by Vālin and where the prince [Sugrīva] resides. (9)
And then Vālin will strive; he will not neglect us, whether by taking refuge with Rāma or by forming an alliance with Rāma.
Śūrpaṇakhā: Now, if Rāma slays Vālī—who has already provoked the enmity of Paraśurāma—then I suspect that the alliance between Vibhīṣaṇa and Rāma will lead to disaster.

Mālyavān: Surely, my child, he who slays Vālin—by him we have been slain; for in that total destruction, it is certain that he alone shall survive as the thread of our lineage. To him, Rāma, who is composed of righteousness, bestows sovereignty. (10)
Śūrpaṇakhā:
(With tears) Let it be so, at least for now.

Mālyavān: Go now, my child, to where you have been sent. This task would be easy to accomplish if Vasiṣṭha and Viśvāmitra were not present near Janaka and Daśaratha. As for me, I too shall go to Laṅkā.
Śūrpaṇakhā: Alas, mother! You too must witness this suffering.
Mālyavān:
Alas, my dear ones, Khara, Dūṣaṇa, and the rest—you are to be slain because of my own sin! Alas, alas, my dear Vibhīṣaṇa, even you stand to be abandoned by me for the sake of my purpose!
Alas, my child Rāvaṇa, who is so devoted to me, I foresee a great calamity for you! My dear Kaikasī, alas, you are destroyed; before long you shall behold your three sons as corpses.
(Thus they both exit. //The Interlude//

(Then Janaka and Daśaratha enter together with Vasiṣṭha and Viśvāmitra. The two kings embrace each other. Janaka: O King, by good fortune you prosper, for such is your dear son Rāmabhadra—extraordinary in his virtues, constant in them, transcendent, and bringing great success through their fruits.
The wonderful deeds of that great hero are auspicious not only for us, but for the entire world as well. //12//
Vasiṣṭha: (Embracing Viśvāmitra) Friend, son of Kuśika,
even we cannot sufficiently praise the greatness and noble lineage of Rāma.
By what [you have done], we and the worlds have become perfected. //13//
Viśvāmitra: This greatness is the result of the ripening of preeminent merit. Who are we to possess such excellence?
Daśaratha: O Blessed One, son of Kuśika, do not speak thus!
The Ādityas: Just as former kings such as Dilīpa and others took refuge with devotion in this sage—the lord of Arundhatī and a mass of splendor—as if he were their own family deity;
even more praiseworthy than the success of those who possess abundant asceticism and whose blessings are true, is this very treasure of auspiciousness that you have become gracious toward us. (14)
Vasiṣṭha said: It is true that Viśvāmitra is such as this.

That immeasurable greatness, which transcends the range of speech or the scope of the mind, and which surpasses all else—this Brahman-sage kindles it here with his splendors; it is difficult to approach and blazes forth. (15)
Viśvāmitra: O venerable son of Mitrāvaruṇa,
if you praise my two gurus, Sanatkumāra and Aṅgiras— who consist of knowledge and ascetic power— then I am indeed truthful, for your words are ever true to their promise.
But for Rāmabhadra, this is no cause for wonder; for his progenitor is the great king Daśaratha.
Indeed, in the lineage of Manu, son of Vivasvat, there have been kings who were like personifications of accumulated merit, protecting their subjects according to the rites prescribed by you.

Among those who existed in the first age, possessed of pure conduct, this hero—the bearer of the burden, the bull among Kṣatriyas, a treasury of virtues, and a praiseworthy lord of the earth—is the very best of them. (17)
Moreover:

Maghavat chose this hero for many battles—him who is the unharmed son of Tvaṣṭṛ in the rite of pacification, the subduer of Jambha, the Lord of All, and even the sovereign of the host of Maruts; the conqueror of armies and the constant destroyer of Asuras. (18)
How can such a thing as this produce something that is not like itself?
Vasiṣṭha: What is there to marvel at here?
The Lord who conquered the god Marutvant here—him, the ten-faced Rāvaṇa, the lord of the Haihayas, defeated in battle.
Having conquered that slayer of [Kārtavīrya] Arjuna, whose greatness is renowned throughout the three worlds and who is a great hero, what indeed has our dear child not conquered? (19)
Daśaratha: Why then does this world split into two factions?

Viśvāmitra: This is the dear child Rāmabhadra, returning this very way along with the son of Jamadagni. He shines with both heroic splendor and humility; he bows before the venerable sage while being exalted by his own virtues.
Bearing shame before the Lord of the Bhṛgus, whose prowess and pride have been taken away, he appears like a disciple who has committed his first offense against his teacher. (20)
(Then enter Rāma and Jāmadagnya. Rāma:
[I bow] to him whose feet are worshipped and praised by those who discourse on the Veda, who is a treasury of knowledge, austerity, and vows, and the most excellent among those who radiate heat.
If, by chance, I have committed an offense against you through a lack of humility, then be gracious toward me, O Blessed One; here is my salutation with joined palms.

Jāmadagnya: You have indeed committed an offense against the son of Jamadagni; you have done him no favor. The holy Brahmin caste, my lineage, my virtues, my sacred scriptures, and my conduct—all these were seized by him alone, who robbed me of even a mere fragment of my consciousness.
Yet, O child, though he was singularly dense with manifold faults, this very disease of pride has been quelled for the sake of peace by you, my dear friend, who are devoted to the Brahmins. (22)
Rāma: How is it that I have not committed an offense, since Duryodhana has already mounted his chariot before I had even taken up my weapons?

The son of Jamadagni said: "This indeed is the proper course for you: having diagnosed the incurable defect of embodied beings, the king, like a physician with sword in hand, provides medical treatment. (23)
Rāma: Who am I in this exchange of questions and answers with the Blessed One? Therefore, let the Blessed One go from here to there.
Jāmadagnya: But where, my child, must I go? Rāma: Where my father and my father Janaka are; or rather, let it be—where the two blessed ones, Maitrāvaruṇa and Kauśika, are.

Jāmadagnya: This is now impossible; yet the command of the king must not be transgressed. (Walking about) O venerable ones! This is that Rāma—gentle in nature, yet fierce despite his lack of ferocity, and possessed of terrible prowess.
He whose victorious command was firmly established even over the son of Jamadagni.
O two kings! Your outpouring of benevolence is exceedingly profound.
Rāma: This is the turn for you to offer salutations with my head bowed.
All: Come, come, dear child!
(Thus they embrace.

Jāmadagnya: Venerable Maitrāvaruṇa, here is the son of Jamadagni, together with Kauśika, bowing down and making this request to your holiness: "May my gurus prescribe an expiation for the great sin accumulated by my transgression against my elders, for me who have been subdued by Rāma."
In former times, you yourselves were the supreme seers of Dharma; having received knowledge from your teacher, Manu and the others promulgated it in various ways through their teachings. //25//

Vasiṣṭha said: Today you have been born into the house of us who are learned in the Vedas. We are miserable because of you, ill-behaved as you are; otherwise, we would be happy. For this is the nature of the elders: that which is for one's welfare is exactly what they do. (26)
Thus, you are indeed completely purified.

Viśvāmitra: We know that your sin has been destroyed by Rāmabhadra; for the teachers of dharma declare that even royal punishment is a means of expiation for an offense, much like a ritual atonement—how much more so when the venerable Vasiṣṭha pronounces judgment here in the presence of the protector of the people?
Rāma: These are those very words of yours, the ṛṣis who have directly realized dharma—words that are serene, profound, and purifying.
Daśaratha: O Blessed One, son of Jamadagni, what else could purify you, who are pure by nature? Neither the water of a sacred ford nor fire requires purification from any other source. (27)
Jāmadagnya:
(To himself) O blessed Earth, be gracious by granting me an opening.
Janaka said: "Venerable sir, if you are pleased, then complete my household by sitting down with confidence; here is a pure seat for the Blessed One."
Jāmadagnya: Whatever is pleasing to you, O disciple of the Sun's pupil, you who are a kṣatriya and a learned śrotriya.
Everyone sits down.

Daśaratha: You have reached the conclusion of your lives outside the inhabited realm, while we too have been preoccupied with our own domestic affairs; thus, that meeting which did not occur has today, through the ripening of our good deeds, been attained by us after a long time as the very object of your heart’s desire. (28)
And here:
What praise can there be for you whose glory transcends the path of praise? And what can be given to one who has bestowed the entire earth without reserve?
O Sage, what need has the peaceful one for attendants? Nevertheless, Daśaratha, together with his sons, is today subject to your will. (29)
Jāmadagnya: That you are such as this—what is there to marvel at?

He whom the wise proclaim as the blazing effulgence, he who is the treasury of lights, that divine Savitṛ is the source of your lineage; what further ground for praise could there be for prosperity than this?
You Ikṣvākus are performers of sacrifice and seekers of the supreme goal, you whose spiritual preceptor in dharma is Vasiṣṭha, whose greatness is immeasurable like the Veda itself. (30)
Moreover:
the bow of the Lord of the Gods, which brings about the desired conclusion of battles; the mountain-caves marked by the rows of herds of deer dwelling in the seven continents;
the divine Bhāgīrathī, the eternal foundation of fame; and the ocean—these various well-known things proclaim the vastness of your domain. (31)
Vasiṣṭha and Viśvāmitra:
(Aside) This too has been learned by our dear child.
Jāmadagnya: O Rāmabhadra, grant me your permission to depart for the forest.
Viśvāmitra: Furthermore, may you grant me leave as well. In the houses of the Raghus and Janakas, I have experienced the auspicious increases resulting from the exchange of infants;
[and I have witnessed] the subduing of the Lord of the Bhṛgus—
(Having stopped after speaking thus halfway:
"And having greeted my dear child, whose greatness is known to the Lord of the Bhṛgus, may I return home in happiness. (32)
Daśaratha: My child Rāmabhadra, the venerable Kauśika has set out for you.
Viśvāmitra, embracing Rāma with tears: "O gentle one, I myself am loath to let you go;
however, the necessity of performing religious duties takes away one's independence.
For the life of a householder who maintains the sacred fires is fraught with difficulties due to the risks of transgression. (33)
Vasiṣṭha says: He may go from his house to his own home or return from it according to his own will.
Viśvāmitra said: "Venerable sir, if you consent, then come; let us both go to Siddhāśramapada. By going with you as my guide, I shall be honored by Madhucchandas’s mother."
Vasiṣṭha: Do you have no power even over us in this matter?

O King, the meeting of these two Brahman-sages, delightful and purifying, shines even in its apparent contradiction—since they are mutually aware of each other’s greatness yet remain unknown to others; if this is so, what need is there to speak of their underlying affection? (34)
(Offstage: Here is Rāma’s wife, saluting her elders.

O child Jānakī! Now that the great terrors of Vṛtra’s slayer have been quelled by your heroic husband, whose conduct is auspiciously disciplined, let Śacī herself mentally offer you the vigorous honor and high esteem due to the wife of a preeminent Kṣatriya. (35)
Rāma:
(To himself) When the Rākṣasas have been thus eradicated root and branch, this shall come to pass.
The Ṛṣis: "May it be well with you, sirs; may it be exactly so.
(They rise. The others:
(Rising) Homage, homage to you!
The son of Jamadagni: Your honors, the son of Jamadagni salutes you.
Vasiṣṭha and Viśvāmitra said:
May your tranquility be firm; may the inner light shine forth;
may your internal organ possess unbroken auspicious resolve. (36)
Thus they both exit.
Jāmadagnya: (Walking about a little and stopping) Dear Rāmabhadra, come this way.
Rāma: (Approaching) Command me.
Jāmadagnya: That which was determined by me, having rested from the destruction of the Kṣatriyas—that very bow now bears a lack of purpose. (37)
Let the axe serve the purpose of providing fuel and the like.
As for those numerous sages who dwell constantly on the banks of rivers in the Daṇḍaka forest—those Rākṣasas residing in Laṅkā roam about there to destroy them;
it would be useful for subduing them. Now, my child, your duty lies with this very bow along with that [axe]. (38)
(He offers it.
Rāma: (Bowing,) This command is accepted.
Jāmadagnya:
(Walking about tearfully) "Long-lived one, turn back! [He exits.]
Rāma:
(With tears) The venerable Bhārgava has departed.
(Reflecting) Even so, might I perhaps set out for the Daṇḍaka forest by some other means? How could this happen even from my elders, who are so dear to Rāma?
While the Lord of the Bhṛgus had laid down his weapons and was thus dependent on others, and while I was likewise so,
alas, the ascetics were driven away by cruel Yātudhānas.
(Offstage: Noble sir, noble sir!
She who is the dear friend of your mother Madhyamā, named Mantharā—she has arrived from Ayodhyā, desiring to see you, O Rāma. (40)
Rāma: Well said; it is fitting that her distress caused by the separation from her young children should be dispelled. Therefore, dear Lakṣmaṇa, approach her.

(Then enter Lakṣmaṇa and Śūrpaṇakhā, disguised as Mantharā. Śūrpaṇakhā: I am Śūrpaṇakhā, possessing the body of Mantharā through my power of transformation. Because Vasiṣṭha has granted me leave to go, I am well-composed. Oh, this Prince Rāma is the conqueror of Paraśurāma! (Gazing at him: Oh, his handsome form is a nectar for the eyes, perfected by the possession of every fortune and grace! Ah, even now it causes my heart to throb again—though that heart has long since cast off the sorrows of worldly existence through the firmness of its character.
Rāma: (Prostrating) Mantharā, is my mother well?

Śūrpaṇakhā: All is well and auspicious. Child, here is your middle mother, with breasts overflowing, embracing you and commanding: "Son, I shall inform the Great King of the two boons previously promised; be the bearer of my petition for that purpose. This is the letter regarding your father's business.
Lakṣmaṇa: (Taking it, he reads:
"By one boon, let dear Bharata enjoy the glory of supreme sovereignty."
(To himself:
How can this be? Noble brother Bharata, the youngest, still harbors a desire for the kingdom while the noble one remains!
(Aloud: Let Rāma go to the Daṇḍaka forest by some other means, avoiding any delay.
(To himself: Alas, Mother! What have you done by obstructing my noble brother’s departure?
(Aloud: Let him remain there for fourteen years wearing bark garments; furthermore, no one other than Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa shall follow as his attendants. (41)

(To herself) Alas, you wicked egg, you kinswoman of my mother! Having abandoned the cry of "Mother" uttered by Bharata, Śatrughna, Lakṣmaṇa, Ārya, and the others, what has been done by you, a sinner? 42.
Rāma: Oh, what a height of grace!
The command to go is given to that very place where my mind is yearning; thus, this separation has not occurred, and my dear younger brother remains with the king. (43)
Lakṣmaṇa: By good fortune, I have been favored with the approval of my noble brother.
Rāma: Noble Mantharā, here I am setting forth.
Śūrpaṇakhā: Homage now to the blessed cycle of existence (saṃsāra), wherein even such wish-fulfilling trees (kappaduma) sprout!
(Thus she exits. Lakṣmaṇa: Ah, my maternal uncle Yudhājit, accompanied by the noble Bharata, approaches our father.
Rāma: By good fortune and yet with sorrow!
Without embracing Bharata, I have no fortitude as I depart; moreover, I cannot bear to look upon him, for he is tormented by the pain of our exile. (44)

(Entering, Yudhājit and Bharata approach Daśaratha: Your Majesty, please listen to that which the subjects, having united as one, report to you: "By the grace of our lord, through this son of yours who is the protector of the three Vedas, we shall today, by means of King Rāmabhadra, become possessed of a true king, attain security, and fulfill our desires. (45)
Daśaratha: Friend Janaka, we have been urged by our subjects who desire what is dear and auspicious;
however, the two sons of Mitra and Varuṇa [Vasiṣṭha] and Kauśika [Viśvāmitra] are not here, for they are dear to Rāma.
Janaka will bring joy to the two of them through his deeds performed out of their sight;
for the venerable Vāmadeva, who is skilled in mantras, is indeed still present there.
Daśaratha: If that is so, then let this very great festival of victory over the son of Jamadagni be joined with the great festival of my consecration.
Rāma: How is this so now?
Daśaratha said: "Sumantra, let the materials for the consecration be brought together; and whoever requires anything, let that person's desire be fully satisfied."
Rāma:
(Approaching and bowing) I, for my part, am a petitioner.
Daśaratha: My child, by whom?
Rāma:
Mother, that very person to whom you entrusted the two boons—him, O Father, our mother Madhyamā now entreats as she pleases; we, for our part, seek his favor. (48)
Daśaratha: The descendants of Raghu are indeed true to their word; why, my child, do you hesitate?
Even if you were merely a messenger, who would value her life as a mere commodity? 49.
Rāma: Child, let it be spoken.
Lakṣmaṇa: (He causes [the king] to recite the words beginning with "Let it be with one boon...").
The others: What, something else entirely? Alas, we are undone!
(The King faints.
Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa: Father, take heart! Janaka:

The wife of that king, the ornament of the Ikṣvāku dynasty, who was born into a pure royal lineage—how could that noble lady commit such a calamitous act of a Rākṣasa? Oh, what a great marvel this is for us! (50)
Rāma: Father, if you are true to your promise, or if Rāma is dear to you, then let our mother be gracious; let the middle one have her desire fulfilled. (41)
Daśaratha: So be it. What recourse is there?
Janaka: Alas, dear Rāmabhadra! Alas, dear Lakṣmaṇa!

That forest-dweller’s vow, which was maintained by the aged Ikṣvākus who had transferred their royal fortune to their sons—that very vow has been undertaken by you, though you are still a mere babe at the breast.
Child Jānakī! You are blessed, for it is solely by the command of your elders that you follow your husband.
Daśaratha: Alas, child Jānakī! Wearing your very bracelets, you have been brought by the Rākṣasas to be offered as a sacrifice.
(Thus both faint. Rāma: My elders have fallen into great peril! How indeed can this be?

Lakṣmaṇa: Noble brother, such is this sudden surge of compassionate affection. What can be done in this matter? Furthermore, our mother Bharata’s mother has forbidden us from wasting time. Therefore, enough of this timidity born of excessive affection.
Rāma: Well done, you who are harsh in your virtuous conduct! Your inner essence is like that of a non-human being. Therefore, my dear child, bring Vaidehī here.
(Lakṣmaṇa exits.
Bharata: Uncle, this is worthy of your household.

Yudhājit: My child, I have become utterly bewildered. My husband enters the jaws of death; this pair of sons and their young bride are offered like a wretched tribute to the Rākṣasas. The world is left without support, its lineage destroyed by infamy, and the wickedness of my sister-in-law agitates the entire world with its distress. (53)
(Then enter Lakṣmaṇa and Sītā. Lakṣmaṇa: Noble brother, here is the noble lady.
Rāma: This way, this way.
Sītā: By good fortune, I am favored by the noble sir.
Rāma:
(Having circumambulated his elders together with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa: Uncle!
Here is my father, here is my grandfather, and here are my mothers, who are so fond of their children.
In this grief, we have come to you alone for consolation. (54)
(Thus they walk about. Yudhājit:
(With agitation) How can I abandon her in the forest?
(Rising and running after him. Bharata:
(Following him) Uncle, tell me, what shall I do now?
Yudhājit: O Rāmabhadra, look upon Bharata, your attendant at your feet and your companion in the forest.
Rāma: Indeed, he too has the heavy duty of protecting the castes and stages of life.
Bharata: Let that belong to Lakṣmaṇa or to Śatrughna.
Rāma: What has anyone's own preference to do with this?
Bharata: This much is my own preference.
Rāma: Ah! Is it possible for you, or anyone else, to transgress what is right while I am standing here?
Bharata: Alas, alas! How am I, unfortunate as I am, being abandoned?
(Thus he faints. Yudhājit: Child, take heart!
Bharata: (Recovering his breath) Uncle, support me!
Yudhājit: My child, let it be so for now.
(Whispering into Bharata's ear: "Rāmabhadra sends this request: 'May my noble brother graciously accept this pair of golden sandals sent by the venerable Śarabhaṅga.'"
Rāma: (Unfastening it) Take this, my child.
Bharata:
(Placing it upon his head) Noble brother!
Rāma:
(Embracing him) Return now by touching my feet; for the moment, honor your two fathers, who have long been bewildered.
Bharata: Now, having been consecrated in Nandigrāma while wearing matted locks upon the sandals of my noble brother, I shall protect the earth until my noble brother returns. (55)
(He circumambulates Sītā and Rāma.
Lakṣmaṇa: Noble brother Bharata, Lakṣmaṇa bows down to you.
(Bharata embraces him and acts out being choked with tears.
Rāma: My child, honor your father.
Bharata: Alas! Even now he has not breathed a sigh of relief.
(Thus he fans her. Janaka:
(Sighing deeply and looking all around: Alas, alas! I have been robbed!
Daśaratha: (Taking a breath) My dear Rāmabhadra, you must not go!
My life-breaths are failing on all sides; I am enveloped in darkness, and unprecedented pains are tearing through my vital organs.
Place the moon of your face near my eyes and give me your voice; alas, my son, do not suddenly be so merciless toward me! //56//
(As if frantic with agitation) Oh, where shall I, unfortunate as I am, enter now?

(Thus, distressed, he exits being led away by Bharata and Janaka. Yudhājit: Dear Rāmabhadra, having united, let us slowly proceed through this place where many people have gathered from various times for a single purpose; where cries have ceased, yet men and women are bewildered here and there, crying out, "What is this?"
But this city of yours is reported to have suddenly become quite otherwise, wherein the roads, being mired with thick showers of tears, are overcast like a rainy day. (57)
Rāma: Uncle, please return; here is Bharata in your care.
Yudhājit: "Obey me; follow after me."
Rāma: Peace! You elders are not to follow me; it is the command of my mother that I am to go with only one other besides myself.

Yudhājit: Why should I go alone? Rather, let the subjects, including the young and the old, go as well. Do you not see these great Brahmins of Sāketa, along with their soldiers, running even though they are elderly—their collections of sacrificial vessels borne upon their shoulders, and these very same men who, with parasols acquired through their own Vājapeya sacrifices, would otherwise have warded off the rays of the sun for you? They run with their wives carrying the sacred fires and their offering-cows having been sent ahead. (58)

Rāma: Uncle, uncle! It is precisely the elders who must protect children from the loss of dharma. Therefore, be gracious to us; turn back and let this great multitude of people be turned back as well.
(Thus he bows. Yudhājit: Child, rise, rise! Having awakened the subjects, I, unfortunate as I am, shall depart for some other place.
You, O mighty-armed Lakṣmaṇa, and you, daughter of the King of Videha— [I leave you both behind.]
I bid you farewell; I have turned back as a sinner. May it be well with you both. //59//
(Stopping her weeping) Oh, how wonderful! This "Commentary on Conduct," the morning purifier for the worlds, shall indeed be sung by all beings throughout every Manvantara. (60)

(Thus he exits. Lakṣmaṇa: The noble one has been informed by Guha, the lord of the Niṣādas residing in Śṛṅgaverapura, regarding the wicked conduct of the Rākṣasa Virādha, who has launched a raid upon the borders of that region.

Rāma: In that case, let us go to Citrakūṭa, the mountain whose girdle is purified by the nearby Mandākinī and which has been approached for the sake of crushing Virādha and Hataka; then, having reached Daṇḍakā where the sages frequent its sacred bathing-places and having slain the Rākṣasas, we shall proceed in due order to Janasthāna, where the king of the vultures resides. 61.
(Thus they all exit. //The Fourth Act//
Bapra.
